text:
“What do you expect, Marguerite? I love you too much, and I am jealous of the least of your thoughts. What you proposed to me just now would drive me mad with joy, but the mystery that precedes the execution of this plan constricts my heart.”

“Come, let us reason a little,” she resumed, taking both my hands and looking at me with a charming smile which it was impossible for me to resist; “you love me, do you not? And you would be happy to spend three or four months in the country alone with me; I too would be happy with this solitude for two; not only would I be happy with it, but I need it for my health. I cannot leave Paris for so long without putting my affairs in order, and the affairs of a woman like me are always very tangled; well, I have found a way to reconcile everything, my affairs and my love for you—yes, for you, do not laugh, I am mad enough to love you! And now you put on your grand airs and say grand things to me. Child, three times a child, just remember that I love you, and do not worry about anything. Is it agreed, then?”

“Whatever you wish is agreed; you know that very well.”

“Then, before a month has passed, we shall be in some village, walking along the water’s edge and drinking milk. It seems strange to you to hear me talk this way, me, Marguerite Gautier; that is because, my friend, when this Parisian life, which seems to make me so happy, does not burn me, it wearies me, and then I have sudden longings for a quieter existence that would remind me of my childhood. One has always had a childhood, whatever one may have become. Oh! Do not worry, I am not going to tell you that I am the daughter of a retired colonel and that I was educated at Saint-Denis. I am a poor country girl, and six years ago I did not know how to write my name. There, you are reassured, are you not? Why are you the first person to whom I turn to share the joy of the desire that has come over me? No doubt because I have recognized that you loved me for myself and not for yourself, whereas the others have never loved me except for themselves.

“I have very often been to the country, but never as I would have wished to go there. I am counting on you for this simple happiness, so do not be unkind, and grant it to me. Tell yourself this: she is not destined to live to old age, and one day I would regret not having done for her the first thing she asked of me, when it was so easy to do.”

What could one answer to such words, especially with the memory of a first night of love, and in expectation of a second?

An hour later, I held Marguerite in my arms, and had she asked me to commit a crime, I would have obeyed her.

At six in the morning I left, and before leaving I said to her:

“Until this evening?”

She embraced me more tightly, but did not answer me.

During the day, I received a letter containing these words:

“Dear child, I am a little unwell, and the doctor orders me to rest. I shall go to bed early this evening and shall not see you. But, to reward you, I shall expect you tomorrow at noon. I love you.”

My first words were: “She is deceiving me!”

An icy sweat passed over my brow, for I already loved this woman too much for that suspicion not to overwhelm me.

And yet, with Marguerite, I ought to have expected such an occurrence almost every day, and it had often happened to me with my other mistresses without my troubling much about it. Whence, then, came the power this woman was gaining over my life?

Then I thought that, since I had the key to her apartment, I would go and see her as usual. In that way I would very soon know the truth, and if I found a man there, I would slap his face.

In the meantime, I went to the Champs-Élysées. I remained there for four hours. She did not appear. In the evening, I went into every theater she habitually attended. She was in none of them.

At eleven o’clock, I went to the Rue d’Antin.

There was no light in Marguerite’s windows. Nevertheless, I rang. The porter asked me where I was going.

“To Mademoiselle Gautier’s,” I told him.

“She has not come home.”

“I shall go upstairs and wait for her.”

“There is no one at her apartment.”

Clearly, these were instructions that I could override, since I had the key, but I feared a ridiculous scene, and I left.

Only, I did not go home; I could not leave the street, and I did not take my eyes off Marguerite’s house. It seemed to me that I still had something to learn, or at least that my suspicions were going to be confirmed.

Around midnight, a coupé that I knew well stopped near number 9.

The Comte de G... stepped out of it and entered the house, after dismissing his carriage.

For a moment I hoped that, as with me, he would be told that Marguerite was not at home, and that I would see him come out again; but at four in the morning I was still waiting.

I have suffered greatly during the past three weeks, but it is nothing, I believe, compared with what I suffered that night.




Chapter XIV


Once home, I began to weep like a child. There is no man who has not been deceived at least once, and who does not know what one suffers.

Under the weight of those feverish resolutions which one always believes one will have the strength to keep, I told myself that I must break off this love immediately, and I waited impatiently for daylight so that I could go and book my seat and return to my father and my sister, a twofold love of which I was certain, and which would not deceive me.

However, I did not wish to leave without Marguerite knowing clearly why I was leaving. Only a man who has definitively ceased to love his mistress leaves her without writing to her.

I composed and recomposed twenty letters in my head.

I had been dealing with a girl like all kept women; I had idealized her far too much; she had treated me like a schoolboy, using, in order to deceive me, a ruse of insulting simplicity; it was clear. My pride then gained the upper hand. I had to leave this woman without giving her the satisfaction of knowing how much this break was making me suffer, and this is what I wrote to her, in my most elegant handwriting and with tears of rage and grief in my eyes:
